title: Knowledge Check 1 - Lessons 1-5
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 1-5 - OmniStudio Fundamentals. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: A consulting team is evaluating OmniStudio for a client that needs a guided multi-step application flow with a reusable data-integration layer. Which statement best describes how the OmniStudio tools relate to each other?
options: Each tool is a standalone product with its own runtime and metadata model.
The tools share one runtime and metadata model and are designed to compose, so a FlexCard can call an OmniScript and an OmniScript can invoke an Integration Procedure.
The tools are only usable independently and cannot reference each other's artifacts.
The tools replace the Salesforce platform's native security and sharing model.
questions.explanation: The defining architectural point of OmniStudio is that FlexCards, OmniScripts, Integration Procedures, and Data Mappers share a single runtime and metadata model and are built to compose. Option A is wrong because they are not standalone products with separate runtimes. Option C is wrong because cross-referencing artifacts is a core feature. Option D is wrong because OmniStudio runs on top of the platform's security model rather than replacing it.

questions.question: A client asks whether OmniStudio can be used to build a guided quote-and-application journey for a high-volume sales team. Which consideration is most important for the architect to communicate about the declarative-first design?
options: OmniStudio requires custom Apex for every step of the journey.
OmniStudio is best suited to high-volume, form-heavy, multi-step processes, and the declarative tools cover the common path while unusual logic still needs Apex.
OmniStudio only works for single-page forms and cannot handle multi-step flows.
OmniStudio bypasses object permissions so any user can see any record.
questions.explanation: OmniStudio's value is strongest for high-volume, form-heavy, multi-step processes where guided steps and reusable components reduce custom page maintenance. Option A is wrong because the common path is declarative, not Apex-heavy. Option C is wrong because multi-step flows are a primary use case. Option D is wrong because OmniStudio respects, not bypasses, the platform security model.

questions.question: A partner plans to build an OmniStudio solution once and install it into many customer orgs. Why does the metadata-based design of OmniStudio support this model?
options: Because OmniStudio artifacts are compiled into a single binary that cannot be reused.
Because every OmniStudio artifact is metadata that can be versioned, deployed through change sets or a DevOps pipeline, and reused across orgs.
Because each customer org must rebuild every artifact from scratch.
Because OmniStudio artifacts are stored only in the customer's browser cache.
questions.explanation: OmniStudio artifacts are metadata, so they can be versioned, deployed through change sets or a DevOps pipeline, and reused across orgs, which is exactly what a build-once-install-many partner model needs. Option A is wrong because there is no single compiled binary. Option C is wrong because reuse across orgs is the point. Option D is wrong because artifacts live in the org's metadata, not the browser cache.

questions.question: A telecom client needs a guided flow where a rep selects a plan, adds devices and add-ons, and hands off to a quote. Which OmniStudio pattern best fits this process?
options: A single FlexCard that displays the final quote only.
An OmniScript that drives the guided plan, add-on, and eligibility steps, with Integration Procedures pulling pricing and eligibility from the billing system.
A Data Mapper used alone to transform the quote payload.
A custom Apex page that bypasses OmniStudio entirely.
questions.explanation: A telco quote-to-order journey is a guided multi-step process, which is exactly what an OmniScript drives, and the pricing and eligibility lookups belong in Integration Procedures. Option A is wrong because a FlexCard alone cannot drive the guided steps. Option C is wrong because a Data Mapper transforms data but does not guide a journey. Option D is wrong because it abandons the declarative value OmniStudio provides for this common pattern.

questions.question: A healthcare client needs a patient intake flow that captures sensitive eligibility and benefits data. What is the most important architectural consideration for this use case?
options: Building custom logic that reads all fields regardless of role.
Ensuring the guided flow respects the platform's security model and field-level access so only authorized roles see sensitive data.
Storing all intake data in a single unencrypted custom object.
Avoiding the platform's sharing rules to simplify the flow.
questions.explanation: Healthcare intake involves sensitive data, so the architect must ensure the flow respects the platform's security model and field-level access. Option A is wrong because bypassing field-level access is a privacy violation. Option C is wrong because it ignores data protection. Option D is wrong because sharing rules are part of the correct access model, not something to avoid.

questions.question: A public-sector client needs a permit application flow that must be auditable. Which approach best supports the auditability requirement?
options: Capturing the submission in a record with a clear audit trail of who submitted what and when.
Storing submissions only in the browser cache.
Allowing any user to edit any submission after it is filed.
Deleting submission history after 30 days to reduce storage.
questions.explanation: Public-sector permit flows need an audit trail, so the architect should capture the submission in a record with clear metadata about who submitted what and when. Option B is wrong because browser cache is not durable or auditable. Option C is wrong because post-filing edits undermine the audit trail. Option D is wrong because deleting history destroys the auditability the process requires.

questions.question: During discovery, a customer says the new OmniScript must return pricing 'instantly' for a quote flow. What is the most important thing for the architect to do with this requirement?
options: Accept it as stated and design for the fastest possible response.
Probe the underlying assumption, such as the source system's actual response time and the latency the business will tolerate, and validate it before it becomes a design constraint.
Ignore the timing requirement because it is not measurable.
Assume the billing system can always respond in under a second.
questions.explanation: An unvalidated assumption like 'instantly' hides a real constraint, the source system's response time and the latency the business tolerates, so the architect must probe and validate it before it becomes a design decision. Option A is wrong because accepting it unexamined risks a design that fails in production. Option C is wrong because timing is measurable and important. Option D is wrong because assuming the billing system's speed is exactly the unvalidated assumption that causes failures.

questions.question: A customer describes a solution in detail, including the exact screens they want. What should the architect do to get at the real project need?
options: Build exactly the screens the customer described.
Walk through real scenarios and sample data to separate what the customer wants from what the process actually needs.
Ask the customer to write the requirements themselves with no further input.
Assume the described solution is the correct one because the customer knows their business.
questions.explanation: Users often describe the solution they imagine rather than the problem they have, so the architect should walk through real scenarios and sample data to separate wants from actual needs. Option A is wrong because building the described screens may solve the wrong problem. Option C is wrong because the architect's elicitation is what surfaces the real need. Option D is wrong because the described solution is not automatically correct.

questions.question: After discovery, the architect has a list of requirements and assumptions. What is the correct way to lock these down before design begins?
options: Keep them in the architect's notes and proceed with design.
Write down the assumptions, confirm them with the customer in writing, and produce a requirements baseline with acceptance criteria that the customer signs off on.
Share them verbally in a meeting and start building.
Wait until after the build to document what was decided.
questions.explanation: Assumptions must be written down and confirmed in writing, and the requirements baseline with acceptance criteria should be signed off before design, because that baseline is what the design is measured against. Option A is wrong because unshared notes do not validate assumptions. Option C is wrong because verbal agreement is not a durable baseline. Option D is wrong because documenting after the build leaves the design unmeasured.

questions.question: A customer has a strict response-time SLA for a quote flow and the source billing system is known to be unreliable. How should the architect classify these two facts?
options: Both are constraints.
The response-time SLA is a constraint, and the source system's reliability is a risk that could break that constraint.
Both are risks.
The response-time SLA is a risk, and the source system's reliability is a constraint.
questions.explanation: The response-time SLA is a hard boundary the design must respect, so it is a constraint, while the source system's reliability is a condition that may or may not occur and could break the SLA, so it is a risk. Option A is wrong because the reliability is not a hard boundary. Option C is wrong because the SLA is a hard boundary, not a may-or-may-not condition. Option D reverses the two classifications.

questions.question: A customer wants a large integration scope delivered on a very tight timeline. What should the architect do about the conflict between these two constraints?
options: Silently prioritize the timeline and cut integration scope without telling the customer.
Surface the conflict and force a decision, because silently trading one off against the other produces a design that fails one of them.
Assume the timeline will slip and plan for a later date.
Ignore the timeline and build the full integration scope.
questions.explanation: Conflicting constraints must be surfaced and a decision forced, because silently trading one off against the other produces a design that fails one of them. Option A is wrong because cutting scope silently fails the integration requirement. Option C is wrong because assuming a slip is not a decision. Option D is wrong because ignoring the timeline fails the schedule constraint.

questions.question: An architect has identified several risks for an OmniStudio project. What is the correct way to handle them?
options: Document them in a register and move on.
Rank them by likelihood and impact, and give the highest-ranked ones a concrete mitigation such as a fallback data path or a phased rollout.
Assume the risks will not occur because the customer is confident.
Only address risks after they happen in production.
questions.explanation: Risks should be ranked by likelihood and impact, and the highest-ranked ones get a concrete mitigation, because a register that only documents problems does nothing to prevent them. Option A is wrong because documenting without mitigating is insufficient. Option C is wrong because confidence is not a mitigation. Option D is wrong because addressing risks only after they occur is too late.

questions.question: A client needs to display a compact account summary on a record page with no user input. Which OmniStudio tool is the right choice?
options: An OmniScript.
A FlexCard.
An Integration Procedure.
A Data Mapper.
questions.explanation: A FlexCard is the reusable, data-driven UI component for displaying a record or set of records, which is exactly the display-only need here. Option A is wrong because an OmniScript is for guided multi-step capture, not display. Option C is wrong because an Integration Procedure is a server-side orchestration with no UI. Option D is wrong because a Data Mapper transforms data rather than displaying it.

questions.question: A client needs a guided, multi-step onboarding flow with validation and branching between steps. Which OmniStudio tool is the right choice?
options: A FlexCard.
A Data Mapper.
An OmniScript.
An Integration Procedure.
questions.explanation: An OmniScript is the guided, multi-step user journey that walks a user through a business process with validation and branching, which is exactly this need. Option A is wrong because a FlexCard displays data rather than guiding steps. Option B is wrong because a Data Mapper transforms data. Option D is wrong because an Integration Procedure is a server-side orchestration without a user interface.

questions.question: A client needs to call an external billing system to fetch pricing, with no user interface involved. Which OmniStudio tool is the right choice?
options: An Integration Procedure.
A FlexCard.
An OmniScript.
A Data Mapper.
questions.explanation: An Integration Procedure is the server-side orchestration for calling external systems, which is exactly a system-to-system pricing call with no UI. Option B is wrong because a FlexCard is a UI display component. Option C is wrong because an OmniScript is a user-facing journey. Option D is wrong because a Data Mapper transforms data rather than making system calls.
